subsystems.name: Reflective membrane
subsystems.role: the mirror itself: a vast, ultra-thin sheet that reflects starlight sideways to create thrust.

subsystems.name: Support and shape structure
subsystems.role: keeps a sheet hundreds of thousands of kilometres across from folding, wrinkling or drifting.

subsystems.name: Station-keeping and attitude control
subsystems.role: holds the mirror at the balance point between gravity and light pressure, and sets the tilt.
parts: small electric or light-pressure trim thrusters

subsystems.name: Thermal and optical management
subsystems.role: sheds the small fraction of light the film absorbs, so it does not warp or melt.

subsystems.name: In-space manufacturing base
subsystems.role: builds and assembles the mirror near the star, since nothing this large can be launched from a planet.

buildSteps.title: Survey the star
buildSteps.detail: Measure its luminosity, activity cycle and radiation environment, and choose which pole the mirror will hover over so the planets keep receiving normal light.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate the statite
buildSteps.detail: Fly a small mirror that holds a fixed point above a body using light pressure alone. Solar sails such as IKAROS (2010) and LightSail 2 (2019) proved photon pressure can push a spacecraft, but no sail has yet hovered motionless against gravity.

buildSteps.title: Get the areal density low enough
buildSteps.detail: For a mirror to hover, it must be extremely light — roughly a fraction of a gram per square metre, meaning a film only a few tenths of a micrometre thick. That is harder than reaching orbit and is the single biggest materials challenge.

buildSteps.title: Source material off-planet
buildSteps.detail: Mine aluminium, silicon and trace metals from asteroids or the Moon and refine them in orbit, because launching the required mass from Earth is impractical.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture the film in space
buildSteps.detail: Roll out and coat the reflective film in microgravity, where it can be handled without sagging under its own weight.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the mirror
buildSteps.detail: Robots join panels one by one, using spin or a sparse tensioned frame to keep the sheet flat. The finished mirror may span hundreds of thousands of kilometres.

buildSteps.title: Move it into the statite point
buildSteps.detail: Slowly bring the mirror to its balance position above the chosen pole, trimming its tilt until gravity and light pressure hold it steady.

buildSteps.title: Tilt and start thrusting
buildSteps.detail: Angle the mirror slightly so the reflected light leaves in one preferred direction. The star recoils the other way, and over millions of years the whole stellar system — star and planets together — drifts through the galaxy.

buildSteps.title: Monitor for the long haul
buildSteps.detail: Track stellar activity, adjust tilt to maintain acceleration, and confirm that planetary climates and orbits are unaffected on human timescales.

prerequisites.why: sails have flown and been steered, but holding a fixed point against gravity using light alone is untested.
nothing approaching a hundreds-of-thousands-of-kilometre sheet has ever been built or deployed.
the mirror must be built from off-world material at a scale far beyond current capability.
self-guided robots would have to assemble millions of panels without human crews.
predicting a star's activity and the system's trajectory over millions of years requires models we do not yet have.

pathway.milestone: solar sails demonstrate photon pressure as measurable thrust
pathway.unlocks: confidence that light alone can push large, thin surfaces.

pathway.milestone: a statite demonstrator hovering at a fixed point above a planet or the Sun
pathway.unlocks: proof that the balance of gravity and light pressure is controllable.

pathway.milestone: kilometre-scale reflectors assembled from mined material in space
pathway.unlocks: practical experience with a fraction of the required build scale.

pathway.milestone: a full one-sided stellar mirror drifting its host star
pathway.unlocks: a theoretical route to moving an entire solar system, measured in millions of years.
